newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian president to ask Socialists to form govt.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian president to ask Socialists to form govt.

text.p: With time running out for mediation in Bulgaria's political deadlock, President Petar Stoyanov promised on Monday to ask the ex-communist ruling Socialists to form a new cabinet as the constitution demands.
Stoyanov, who inherited the crisis when he took office last Wednesday, has tried to find a formula to defuse daily opposition protests now in their fourth week.

But the Socialists and the opposition remain as far apart as ever, and under the constitution Stoyanov is obliged to ask the Socialists, as the biggest party in parliament, to form a new cabinet, which must then be approved by parliament.

Socialist party leader Georgi Parvanov said after talks with Stoyanov that the president had promised to give them a mandate to form a new cabinet before he leaves for a visit to Brussels on Tuesday evening.
"We agreed that before his departure for Brussels, he will hand us a mandate for forming a strong experts' government," Parvanov said.
Stoyanov was meeting other political leaders and promised to address the nation later in the day.
The Socialists insist on nominating Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev as prime minister to replace Zhan Videnov who resigned on December 21.
But he is unacceptable to the opposition who hold him responsible for clashes between police and demonstrators outside parliament on January 10.
The Socialists say their cabinet will be made up of technocrats and have broad public support -- a promise which Stoyanov has warned may be wishful thinking in the current political climate.
The opposition has held daily protests around the country since January 6 to call for immediate elections, while the Socialists have proposed polls by the end of 1997 -- a year ahead of schedule.
If parliament votes on a new Socialist cabinet, the opposition will be pinning its hopes on defections from the majority party.
The vote is almost certain to attract demonstrations, which risk turning violent as they did on January 10, when the opposition besieged and ransacked the legislature.
A general strike called by the main opposition trade union Podkrepa had almost no immediate effect, and the union's call for a human chain around parliament drew about 25 people.

The protests are more economic than political, and an opinion poll in the 24 Hours daily on Monday said 70 percent of those questioned did not trust the Socialists, but 35 percent did not think the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces could cope with the crisis either.
Kontinent daily quoted former communist leader Todor Zhivkov as saying there could be bread riots within the next two months if nothing was done to resolve the crisis.

The national currency is in freefall and January inflation is expected to hit 50 percent per month. The lev traded at new lows of 935-950 to the dollar on the interbank market on Monday, compared to about 750 a week earlier.

Bulgaria urgently needs a credible government to negotiate a new accord with the International Monetary Fund, which has suspended disbursements because the Socialist government failed to implement the last reform programme.
